claim: A loaded 5,000-tonne goods train at 75 km/h needs more than 900 m to stop [OUR CALCULATION, illustrative] (on-screen 5,000 T · 75 KM/H · ≈ 930 M · ILLUSTRATIVE)
source_quote: kilometer per hour (km/h) meter per second (m/s) 2.777 778 E-01
note: Re-run: v = 75/3.6 = 20.83 m/s; 10 s equivalent brake delay = 208 m; v²/2a with a = 0.30 m/s² = 723 m; total 932 m. The 0.30 m/s² and 10 s are assumptions (VO says 'fair guesses', screen says ILLUSTRATIVE): fair. v² method: https://railwaynews.net/wiki/train-braking-distance-how-long-does-a-train-take-to-stop : "Because speed is squared, doubling a train’s speed does not double its braking distance — it quadruples it." Real loaded-freight stops can be longer, so 'more than nine hundred metres' is a floor, not a maximum. v2: V025.
